lessons.title: Slope from a handful of rows
explanation: Full-batch gradient descent averages the slope over every training row. Honest, expensive, and smooth. A minibatch estimates that same slope from a handful of examples. One-row stochastic uses a single example. All three step opposite an estimate of ∇J.

Cost versus noise is the comparison. Full-batch is one accurate direction per pass and a full scan of the data. Stochastic is cheap and noisy: the path jitters, which can escape sharp holes and can also stall. Minibatch sits in between: less noisy than one row, cheaper than the whole set.

A batch of 32 is not a smaller test set. It is a noisier gradient. Shuffle so the handful is not a clump of yesterday's rows. If the batch is the whole dataset, you are back at full-batch. If it is one row, you are at SGD. Pick the noise you can afford.
lessons.example: Ten thousand rows. Full-batch: one gradient from all ten thousand. Minibatch 32: about 312 noisy steps per pass. SGD: ten thousand tiny noisy steps. Same loss, three prices for the slope.
lessons.whyItMatters: People call every walk 'gradient descent'. The handful versus the whole set is the cost and the noise, and they are not the same walk.

quiz.stem: A minibatch gradient is best described as which of these objects?
quiz.correctAnswer: An estimate of the slope from a handful of examples, not from the whole set

distractors.text: The exact full-data gradient, just written with a smaller α
distractors.rationale: A handful is an estimate. α is not the batch.

distractors.text: A locked test split you may report after each step
distractors.rationale: A batch is a training handful, not a test.

distractors.text: A probability squash applied to the residual
distractors.rationale: This lesson is about how you estimate ∇J.

quiz.correctExplanation: Handful in, noisy slope out. That is the minibatch.
objectiveIds: Estimate the slope from a minibatch instead of the whole dataset

quiz.stem: Compare full-batch, one-row SGD, and a minibatch of 32 on cost and noise:
quiz.correctAnswer: Full-batch is smooth and expensive; SGD is cheap and jittery; 32 sits between them

distractors.text: Full-batch is the noisiest; SGD is the most expensive scan
All three have identical noise and identical cost per step
distractors.rationale: The whole point is the trade.

distractors.text: Only full-batch may step opposite the gradient
distractors.rationale: All three step opposite an estimate of ∇J.

quiz.correctExplanation: Cost up, noise down as the handful grows. 32 is the usual middle.
objectiveIds: Compare full-batch, stochastic, and mini-batch updates on cost and noise

quiz.stem: Why shuffle before you cut minibatches, rather than taking yesterday's rows as one clump?
quiz.correctAnswer: A clump is a biased handful, so the slope is not a draw from training P

distractors.text: Shuffling turns the batch into a legal test report
Without a clump the gradient cannot be computed at all
distractors.rationale: You can compute a bad gradient on a clump.

distractors.text: Clumps are required for the walk to be convex
distractors.rationale: Convexity is the loss shape, not the batch order.

quiz.correctExplanation: Shuffle, then a handful. Otherwise the slope is yesterday, not the set.
objectiveIds: Estimate the slope from a minibatch instead of the whole dataset

lessons.title: Independent until the data lies
explanation: Independent, identically distributed examples are the assumption: each row is a fresh draw from the same P, and knowing one row does not tell you the next. Splits, generalization numbers, and 'shuffle then cut' all lean on that claim.

Real data lies. Time series: tomorrow depends on today, so a random split puts the future in train. Users with many rows: the same person leaks across train and test. Hospitals, cameras, or days as clumps: identically distributed is false. The test number then estimates a P you will not see.

A common repair is to split on the clump, not the row: by user, by day, by patient. That keeps the dependence inside a split. It does not make the data i.i.d. It only stops the original sin of reporting a leak as generalization. Name the violation before you shuffle.
lessons.example: A user with 40 sessions. Shuffle-and-cut puts 30 in train and 10 in test. The model has already met that user. A user-level split would have put all 40 on one side.
lessons.whyItMatters: The most common 'great test score' in production data is a person, a day, or a future timestamp that snuck across the cut.

quiz.stem: The i.i.d. assumption, as this lesson states it, says examples are:
quiz.correctAnswer: A fresh draw from one P, with no row telling the next

distractors.text: Dependent on the previous row, and drawn from a new P each time
distractors.rationale: That is the violation, not the assumption.

distractors.text: Required to have a convex loss before any split is legal
distractors.rationale: i.i.d. is about the rows, not the bowl.

distractors.text: Always shuffled into the test drawer after each epoch
distractors.rationale: A ritual is not the assumption.

quiz.correctExplanation: Independent, identical, one P. That is the claim the split leans on.
objectiveIds: State the i.i.d. assumption: independent, identically distributed examples

quiz.stem: A user with 40 sessions is randomly split 30/10 into train and test. The i.i.d. lie is that:
quiz.correctAnswer: The same person leaked across the cut, so test is not a new draw from P

distractors.text: Forty sessions prove the rows were independent
distractors.rationale: Many rows from one person are dependence.

distractors.text: User-level splitting is illegal in supervised learning
distractors.rationale: Splitting on the clump is the repair.

distractors.text: The logistic curve cannot run on repeated users
distractors.rationale: The crime is the split, not the squash.

quiz.correctExplanation: Same user, both sides. That is not a fresh draw. Split on the person.
objectiveIds: Name a common way real data violates it and what that does to the split

quiz.stem: A random shuffle of a time series puts future rows in train and past rows in test. Diagnose the split:
quiz.correctAnswer: Tomorrow depended on today, so the cut leaked the future and the test number is not tomorrow

distractors.text: Shuffle-and-cut is always legal, because i.i.d. is a style preference
distractors.rationale: Time is a dependence the shuffle ignores.

distractors.text: The series became i.i.d. once you locked a test drawer
distractors.rationale: A lock does not undo time.

distractors.text: You must switch to squared error before a time split is defined
distractors.rationale: The loss is not the dependence.

quiz.correctExplanation: Time is dependence. A random cut puts the future in train. Split by time instead.
objectiveIds: Name a common way real data violates it and what that does to the split
